title: Automatic Differentiation: The Chain Rule as an Algorithm
summary: How reverse-mode automatic differentiation turns any program into exact gradients: record a computational graph, then apply each operation's local derivative in reverse topological order, accumulating over every path.
takeaways: Every computation is a graph of elementary operations, and each one knows its local derivative.
Reverse mode gets the gradient of one scalar loss with respect to every input in a single backward pass.
Gradients from different uses of a value add up: use +=, never =.
Visit nodes in reverse topological order, and check results against finite differences.

steps.label: Forward
steps.detail: Run the program; every operation creates a node that remembers its inputs.

steps.label: Sort
steps.detail: Topologically order the graph so every node comes after its inputs.

steps.label: Propagate
steps.detail: In reverse order, each node adds local derivative × its grad into each input's grad.

steps.label: Use & reset
steps.detail: Read the leaf gradients for the update, then zero them before the next step.

terms.definition: A DAG whose nodes are intermediate values and whose edges record which values each operation consumed.
AD that propagates adjoints ∂L/∂node from the output back to the inputs; backpropagation is a special case.
The derivative of one operation's output with respect to one of its inputs, e.g. 1 − tanh² for tanh.
An ordering of a DAG's nodes in which every node appears after all of its inputs.
Comparing analytic gradients with central finite differences (f(x+h) − f(x−h)) / 2h.
